solution:
**(C)** interkinesis

After cytokinesis-I, the two daughter cells usually pass through a short resting phase called interkinesis, and then meiosis-II begins, so interkinesis is the link between the two divisions. Anaphase-I is a stage inside meiosis-I, not something between the divisions. 'Interphase-I' and 'interphase-II' are not stages the chapter names; the resting phase between the two meiotic divisions is called interkinesis.

**(D)** homologous chromosomes

In zygotene of prophase-I, homologous chromosomes (one maternal, one paternal) pair closely by forming the synaptonemal complex, and this pairing is called synapsis. Non-homologous chromosomes do not pair, and sister chromatids are already joined at the centromere, so their joining is not synapsis.

**(A)** Prophase.

Prophase includes the migration of centrioles and the appearance of the mitotic (spindle) apparatus, and by the end of prophase the mitotic apparatus is almost completely formed. In metaphase the spindle is only completing and its fibres attach to the centromeres. In anaphase the spindle pulls the chromosomes apart, and in telophase the spindle fibres break down.

**(B)** S-phase

In S-phase, DNA is replicated, so the amount of DNA per cell doubles and each chromosome now has two sister chromatids. The question's 'chromosome number' should be read as the DNA content: the chromatids stay joined at one centromere, so the count of chromosomes does not actually change. \(\text{G}_1\) and \(\text{G}_2\) are growth phases, and \(\text{G}_0\) is a non-dividing resting state.

[Note: the chapter does not state this; standard biology gives that only DNA content and chromatid number double in S-phase, while chromosome number stays the same.]

**(C)** 20

One meiosis (meiosis-I followed by meiosis-II) turns one diploid cell into four haploid cells, and each of these develops into a sperm. So 80 sperms need 80 ÷ 4 = 20 meiotic divisions. Here one 'meiotic division' means one complete meiosis of a single parent cell.

**(D)** 40

In anaphase-I the homologous chromosomes move apart, but the two sister chromatids of each chromosome stay joined by their common centromere. The cell still has 20 chromosomes, each with 2 chromatids, so there are 20 × 2 = 40 chromatids. The figure 20 counts chromosomes, not chromatids.

**(B)** Metaphase

In metaphase the fully condensed chromosomes all lie at the equatorial plane of the cell, forming the metaphase plate, with spindle fibres attached to their centromeres. In prophase the chromosomes are only condensing, in anaphase they move to the poles, and in telophase they are at the poles.

**(C)** Daughter nuclei are formed at metaphase.

This statement is incorrect: daughter nuclei form in telophase, when the nuclear membrane and nucleolus reappear around each group of chromosomes. In metaphase the chromosomes are simply lined up at the equator. The other statements are correct: chromatin condenses in prophase, the nuclear membrane reappears in telophase, and in anaphase the chromatids of each chromosome separate to become daughter chromosomes (strictly, the chromatids themselves were formed earlier, when DNA was copied in S-phase).

**(B)** S-phase

The chapter states that histone proteins are synthesized in S-phase, alongside DNA replication, so the new DNA can be packed into chromatin. Interphase is the larger stage that contains S-phase, so it is not wrong, but the question asks for the specific phase. \(\text{G}_1\) is mainly for RNA, protein and membrane synthesis, and \(\text{G}_2\) for the proteins needed for cell division.
